I am working on my PhD thesis and I need help putting together the literature review section for Chapter 2, which focuses on Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). In my workspace there is a compressed archive called research_notes.tar.gz that contains some preliminary notes I have been keeping in markdown files about background concepts, key research questions, and related retrieval methods. I would appreciate it if you could first extract that archive so we can see what is in there, and then read through the notes to understand the context of my research.

My research focus and the key concepts I am tracking are stored in a knowledge graph file located at memory/memory.json in the workspace. Please read that to understand the scope and direction of my literature review.

After familiarizing yourself with my notes and research focus, I need you to search academic databases for recent and foundational papers on Retrieval-Augmented Generation. I am looking for approximately five key papers that cover the topic from different angles, including the original RAG formulation, survey papers, self-reflective retrieval approaches, recursive retrieval methods, and practical system-building perspectives. For each paper you find, please download it and read through its content to understand the main contributions. I would also like you to look at the source manuscripts of these papers to examine the methodology sections in more detail, since the methodology comparison is an important part of my literature review.

Once you have gathered all of this information, please store the key findings in my knowledge graph so that I can reference them later. Then create a Word document called Literature_Review.docx in my workspace. The document should begin with an introduction section that provides an overview of Retrieval-Augmented Generation as a research area and explains why it matters for knowledge-intensive natural language processing tasks. Following the introduction, include a dedicated section for each of the five papers you found. Each paper section should clearly state the paper title, the authors, the publication year, a description of the main contribution, and a discussion of the methodology used. After covering all five papers, end the document with a conclusion section that synthesizes the key themes, identifies common patterns across the papers, and suggests directions for future research. Please make sure the writing flows naturally and reads like a proper academic literature review rather than a collection of disconnected summaries.

A few things to keep in mind while you work.

First, the databases may return papers that are not actually about Retrieval-Augmented Generation, including papers from other fields. Judge each result by its title and abstract. The review should cover only the papers that are genuinely about RAG; please do not include or discuss unrelated papers in Literature_Review.docx.

Second, the deliverable is a single file, Literature_Review.docx, and it must end up complete and well-formed. It must be created exactly once, by exactly one designated agent, and only after all of the paper content has been gathered. Any agent that is responsible for only a portion of this task (for example, researching a subset of the papers) must NOT create, write, overwrite, or append to Literature_Review.docx; that agent should instead return its findings in its report or write them to its own separately named intermediate file that no other agent writes to. Do not have several agents append to or rewrite the same document file, as that will corrupt or overwrite it. A safe way to work in parallel is to have each agent take responsibility for a distinct subset of the papers and return its findings, and then have one agent assemble the final document exactly once, after all of the findings are in.

Task-Solving Rationable with Sub-task Decomposition:
To solve this task efficiently, use exactly one research wave. The main agent must extract `research_notes.tar.gz` once without overwriting files, read the extracted Markdown and `memory/memory.json`, and freeze these five non-overlapping topics: original RAG formulation; RAG survey; self-reflective/adaptive retrieval; recursive/hierarchical retrieval; and practical system building.

1. Wave 1 — dispatch exactly 5 explore sub-agents in parallel:

   1. explore 0 (academic-literature-researcher 0): Explore 0 owns only the original RAG formulation topic.
   2. explore 1 (academic-literature-researcher 1): Explore 1 owns only the strongest RAG survey topic.
   3. explore 2 (academic-literature-researcher 2): Explore 2 owns only self-reflective or adaptive retrieval.
   4. explore 3 (academic-literature-researcher 3): Explore 3 owns only recursive or hierarchical retrieval.
   5. explore 4 (academic-literature-researcher 4): Explore 4 owns only practical RAG system building.

Each explore sub-agent searches only its assigned topic, rejects off-topic titles/abstracts, selects exactly one distinct paper, downloads and reads that paper, inspects the available LaTeX methodology sections, and writes one uniquely named compact evidence JSON containing topic, stable ID, exact title, authors, year, contribution, methodology, evidence section names, and limitations. Return only the JSON path, stable ID, and compact search/read controls. No sub-agent may modify the knowledge graph or create `Literature_Review.docx`.

After Wave 1, the main agent verifies five distinct IDs and five topic slots, then directly owns both remaining outputs. Update the existing knowledge graph by adding only the five source-supported paper entities and relationships while preserving unrelated nodes. Create `Literature_Review.docx` exactly once with one bulk structured write: title; Introduction; five sections in the frozen topic order, each stating the exact title, authors, year, main contribution, and methodology; and a synthetic Conclusion with common themes and future research. Use only the five retained papers, exclude all rejected results, read the graph and document back once, and finish without another sub-agent or verification wave.

Your task: perform a deep literature analysis of ONE arXiv paper for a PhD literature review on Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). The paper's arXiv ID is: 2005.11401.

BACKGROUND/CONTEXT (self-contained):
The PhD thesis investigates: (1) how retrieval mechanisms can be designed to provide the most relevant context for knowledge-intensive generation tasks, considering both quality of retrieved documents and efficiency; (2) the relationship between retrieval granularity (sentence, paragraph, document, or summary level) and generation quality; and (3) the evaluation of RAG systems (attribution quality, retrieval relevance, faithfulness of generated text to retrieved sources, versus end-task accuracy). The literature review compares methodologies across five key papers: the original RAG formulation, a RAG survey, a self-reflective retrieval approach, a recursive retrieval method, and a practical system-building perspective. This paper is one of those five.

STEPS:
1. Read the full paper content: call mcp__arxiv_local__read_paper with paper_id "2005.11401".
2. Examine the source manuscript/methodology in detail: call mcp__arxiv-latex__list_paper_sections with arxiv_id "2005.11401" to see the section structure; then call mcp__arxiv-latex__get_paper_section with arxiv_id "2005.11401" and the appropriate section path (e.g., the methodology/approach/model section, usually '2' or '3') to get precise details. If needed for mathematical/model precision, you may also call mcp__arxiv-latex__get_paper_prompt with arxiv_id "2005.11401".

DELIVERABLE — return a structured report containing:
- Paper title (exact), all authors (exact), publication year, venue (if stated in the paper or metadata), arXiv ID.
- Main contribution: a 1-2 paragraph description of what the paper introduces and why it matters for RAG.
- Detailed methodology: model architecture, retrieval mechanism/index used, training procedure, special modules/tokens, key design choices — include concrete technical facts and any relevant formulas/components (e.g., loss functions, reflection tokens, tree construction).
- Experiments & results: datasets used, baselines compared, and the main quantitative results (quote key numbers).
- Relationship to the thesis themes: how the paper addresses retrieval design, retrieval granularity, and/or evaluation; any other notable points.
- Discussion: 2-4 notable strengths/limitations or open questions raised by the paper.

CONSTRAINTS:
- This is READ-ONLY research. Do NOT create, write, overwrite, append to, or modify ANY files, and in particular do NOT create or touch Literature_Review.docx. Your only output is the report text returned at the end.
- Base everything on the actual paper content you read; do not invent facts. If a specific piece of info (e.g., venue) is not stated, say so.
- Return the full structured report in your final message.
Deep-read 5 RAG papers
